title: The Moon Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: The Moon upright: uncertainty, intuition; reversed: confusion lifting. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Draw it for your question.
image_alt: The Moon, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a yellow moon with a face in profile shines between two gray towers; a dog and a wolf look up at it, and a crayfish climbs out of a pool.
capsule: The Moon is card XVIII of the Major Arcana: uncertainty, intuition, dreams, and also illusion and fear. Reversed, the haze starts to lift, or worry runs ahead of the facts. It is a dim card, not a dark one, and it asks for patience. With the path only half lit, the yes-or-no answer is not clear yet.

blocks.heading: What is on The Moon card?
paragraphs: A large moon fills the top of the card, with a face drawn in profile inside it. Waite says it "is increasing on what is called the side of mercy, to the right of the observer" and has "sixteen chief and sixteen secondary rays" (p. 140). On the 1909 card the moon is yellow, the face has its eyes closed, small yellow drops fall from it, and XVIII stands above.

Below are two gray towers, and between them a path runs from the water up into distant hills. Waite calls it "the issue into the unknown" (p. 140). A dog and a wolf face each other across the path, heads raised; for Waite they are "the fears of the natural mind" facing that way out, "when there is only reflected light to guide it" (p. 140). On the 1909 card the dog is orange and the wolf a pale yellow.

In the foreground a crayfish climbs out of a pool. Waite describes something that comes "up out of the deeps" and tries to reach the land, but "as a rule it sinks back whence it came" (pp. 140, 143). Over all of this, he writes, "The face of the mind directs a calm gaze upon the unrest below", and the message of the card is "Peace, be still" (p. 143).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about The Moon?
paragraphs: The upright list gathers what cannot be seen well: things kept out of view, mistakes, being misled. The reversed list is milder: unsteadiness, changeable moods, silence, smaller errors. Arcana Diary reads those darker upright words only as uncertainty, a stretch when it is easy to misread what you see.

Waite's own view of the card is quieter. He saw in it "life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit", and wrote that "The intellectual light is a reflection" (p. 140). Beyond that light, he adds, lies a mystery it cannot show (p. 140).

blocks.heading: What does The Moon mean upright?
paragraphs: A path under moonlight can stand for uncertainty: a stretch when things are not fully visible yet, and feelings, hints and half-formed worries blur together. It often shows up while you are waiting for information, or when your mind fills the gaps with guesses.

The Moon has a harder side as well: illusion, fear and anxiety, and the chance that something is not what it seems, whether a secret, a half-truth or a story you tell yourself. The card does not say who is mistaken; it says the light is poor.

The card also honors intuition and dreams. They are good at shaping questions (what am I sensing? what keeps coming back?) and less reliable as conclusions. The path on the card is real; it is just lit by a softer light than you would like.
Move slowly and check what is real before acting. Hidden feelings, your own included, may be part of the picture. What are you feeling that you have not named yet?

blocks.heading: What does The Moon mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, The Moon can point to confusion lifting: something you avoided looking at becomes easier to see, a secret or half-truth comes into the open, fears ease and the fog thins. It can also mean worry running ahead of the facts, when the mind fills the dark with more than is there.

Waite's reversed list speaks of instability and "lesser degrees of deception and error" (p. 286), which is near the first reading: the haze is still there, only thinner. Worry outrunning the facts is today's reading rather than Waite's.
Either way, clearer sight comes from separating two lists: what you know and what you only imagine. Let the second list wait for better light.

blocks.heading: What does The Moon mean in love?
paragraphs: Mixed signals call for patience under The Moon. Notice what you feel, ask openly instead of guessing, and give trust time to grow; inside a relationship, the card can describe a stretch when things feel unclear between you, with insecurity, jealousy or the sense that something is being left unsaid.

Single for now? Then it can point to attraction mixed with uncertainty, or to daydreams about someone that are still mostly your own imagining, an idealized picture that may not match the real person.
A misunderstanding clearing, or worry building stories faster than facts: either can be the reversed Moon. What do you actually know, and what have you only assumed?

blocks.heading: What does The Moon mean for work and money?
paragraphs: Work under The Moon tends to come with unclear information: plans still taking shape, instructions open to interpretation, a situation you cannot quite read yet. Asking questions and writing things down beat acting on assumptions.

As a money card, The Moon means unclear terms and hidden details: fine print, costs nobody mentioned, a deal that looks better in dim light than in daylight, or money worries that grow bigger in the dark. Clarity first, choices second.
When the card is reversed, a confusing matter at work may be starting to clear; use that moment to confirm the details.

blocks.heading: What is The Moon's advice?
paragraphs: Wait for clearer light: write down what you know and what you only fear. Keep those two lists apart and act only on the first. Read them again later and see which one has changed.

blocks.heading: Is The Moon a yes or no card?
The Moon as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: Mixed feelings are The Moon's answer when the question turns to love: attraction tangled with uncertainty, insecurity, emotions kept hidden or not yet understood even by the one who has them. It can also mean an idealized picture, someone seen through a romantic haze rather than as they are. Emotionally, it is like walking at night, unease mixed with intuition. Reversed, the haze clears: hidden feelings come into the open, fears ease, or a confusing situation finally makes sense; at times it is a worry that keeps circling. The figure the card draws is someone hard to read, mysterious or changeable, and also the dreamer in you, the part that senses more than it can explain.

pairs.text: Uncertainty giving way to clarity. Wait for daylight before you decide.
A choice made harder by poor visibility. Gather one more fact before you pick a side.
Worries that grow in the dark. Write them down; on paper they often look smaller.
Walking away by moonlight. Make sure you know what you are leaving, and why.

blocks.heading: The Moon or The High Priestess?
paragraphs: Both cards deal with what is not fully in view. In Waite's description of the High Priestess, a crescent moon lies at her feet and her mantle half hides a scroll, so that part of its teaching is said and part only hinted (p. 76); her modern sense is intuition and inner knowing, calm and still. The Moon is the restless version: a path at night, animals calling, shapes hard to make out. The High Priestess knows quietly; The Moon is still finding out.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about The Moon
paragraphs: What do I actually know about this, and what am I only guessing?
Which feeling have I been keeping out of sight, even from myself?
What would I ask if I let intuition shape the question rather than the answer?

faq.q: Is The Moon a good or bad card?
faq.a: Not a bad card: a card of low visibility. It is no sign that something is wrong, only that the full picture is not in view yet. It supports patience, imagination and listening to hunches. What it asks you not to do is treat a guess as if it were a fact.

faq.q: Does The Moon mean someone is lying to me?
faq.a: Not necessarily. The card can carry that meaning: Waite's old list does include deception (p. 286), and modern readings link The Moon to illusion and secrets. More often, though, it points to information you are missing or an assumption you are leaning on, and it never says who is mistaken. A calm, direct question usually helps more than suspicion.

faq.q: What are the drops falling from the moon?
faq.a: Waite calls them dew. In Part I he notes that in nearly all versions the moon is "shedding the moisture of fertilizing dew in great drops" (p. 27). In the card's own entry he adds that "the dew of thought falls" (p. 143) while the mind looks down without alarm at the restless creatures below.

faq.q: Is The Moon a sign to trust my intuition?
faq.a: Partly. The card values intuition, but it also shows how easily shapes are misread at night. Use your hunches to choose what to look into, then compare them with what you can confirm in daylight. Intuition is the lantern here, not the map.

faq.q: Does The Moon mean he loves me?
faq.a: It is an uncertain answer rather than a no. The Moon describes feelings that are real but unclear: attraction mixed with doubt, emotions not yet spoken, a picture of the other person colored by imagination. Reversed, the card means such feelings moving into daylight. Patience and honest questions serve better here than conclusions.

waite.quote: Hidden enemies, danger, calumny, darkness, terror, deception, occult forces, error. Reversed: Instability, inconstancy, silence, lesser degrees of deception and error.
